note.verdict: Weak. Full protection buys 18% of the index's upside, because at a 2.00% rate there is almost nothing left over after guaranteeing the capital. Bought as a retail product the fee takes it to 0%. This structure worked at 4% rates; it does not work at these.

safe.caveat: Everything here assumes the standing tax simplification the rest of the site uses. In practice Irish tax treats a fund, a bill and a deposit differently, and for a five-month holding the difference is small but not nothing. Minimum sizes are as listed on the broker and change by issue; confirm on the ticket before sending it.

rows.title: Factor tilts the long-run record pays for, in reverse
rows.what: The regression measures this book's style exposures, and two of them are significantly negative: size -0.28 (t -5.2), value -0.33 (t -4.5). Valued at conservative long-run premia - half the published figures, because every premium has shrunk since it was published - that is EUR -487 a year against you.
rows.fix: Being short quality means owning loss-makers and diluters; the accounts panel names them. Tilting back does not mean buying a factor fund - it means the next euro goes to the profitable end of what is already on the list, and the dilution flags stop being ignored.

rows.title: Commission on trades too small to carry it
rows.what: This month's orders move EUR 30,116 and pay EUR 164 to do it - 0.5% of the amount traded. At 60% turnover a year that is EUR 170 annually, before the market does anything. The worst single order is AQLT.DE at 1.0%: a fixed minimum commission is a percentage that grows as the trade shrinks.
rows.fix: Set a floor on order size so nothing pays more than 1% to trade, and let the small positions leave in one combined exit rather than five monthly ones. No order this month is over the line.

rows.title: Irish wrapper rules, unpriced
rows.what: A 7% gross return over 10 years is 5.12% a year after tax in shares and 4.65% in a UCITS ETF: exit tax at a higher rate, no loss relief, no annual exemption, and a disposal deemed to happen every eight years whether or not you sell. On the 50% of this book held in funds that gap is EUR 123 a year.
rows.fix: Modelling is on: the expected returns behind the plan are already net of the wrapper.

rows.title: Cash earning nothing
rows.confidence: certain on inflation, high on rate
rows.what: EUR 1,250 is parked. Keeping 3 months of the monthly buy back as a buffer leaves EUR 50 idle. At a 2.00% deposit rate that forgoes EUR 1 a year, and inflation at 3% takes EUR 38 of what it can buy whatever it earns.
rows.fix: Cash for a dated goal belongs in the safe sleeve, where it earns the short rate; cash with no date belongs invested. Cash in a current account is the only holding on this site with a guaranteed negative real return.

rows.title: Ongoing fund charges
rows.what: EUR 36 a year across 4 fund line(s), the largest being AWLD.AS at 0.20%. The same exposure at the cheapest charge in the universe would cost EUR 0.
rows.fix: Fund charges come out of NAV daily and never appear on a statement, which is why they are the easiest cost to ignore and the only one that is certain. Where two funds track the same index, the cheaper one wins by the difference, every year, for ever.

leaks.verdict: About EUR 855 a year, 1.6% of the book, is leaking before the market does anything - and EUR 368 of it (0.7%) is under your control this month rather than next decade. For scale: the equity risk premium anyone is hoping to earn is about 4.5% a year, with a standard error wide enough to swallow a decade. These are certain. Fix them first.
leaks.caveat: Commission and fund charges are arithmetic. The tax figure is a projection at 7% gross over the stated horizon under current Irish rules. The factor cost values measured, statistically significant loadings at deliberately conservative long-run premia - half the published in-sample figures - and is the least certain line here; a tilt is a cost only if the premium survives, and it is shown so the exposure is priced rather than ignored. None of this is a forecast of the portfolio.

current.verdict: Market beta 1.14: for every 1% the world index moves, this book moves about 1.14%. The market alone explains 87% of the book's weekly variance; market plus style explains 90%. The tilts that are real, not noise: size -0.28, value -0.33. The residual - what selection added - annualises to -0.3%, which is not distinguishable from zero. The 10% of variance the factors do not explain is risk being carried without evidence of being paid for it.

factors.caveat: Tilts, not academic factors: each style is a factor ETF's return less the World index, in euro, on weekly returns over three years - weekly because the European factor lines close hours before the US names, and daily data smears every co-movement across two days. Loadings with a t-statistic under two are shown but should be read as zero. The residual is everything the factors do not explain - selection, and luck, in a proportion this sample cannot separate.

rows.label: Holding-period return, whole window
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: Total return over 5.0 years, compounded. The one number that cannot be annualised away.

rows.label: Arithmetic mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The mean weekly return, compounded to a year. The right expectation for a single period ahead; the wrong one for many.

rows.label: Geometric mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The compound rate the money actually grew at. Always at or below the arithmetic mean; the gap is volatility drag, about half the variance.

rows.label: Arithmetic less geometric (volatility drag)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: What the swings cost the compounding. This is the number the 'smoothest ride' mix on Advice is buying down.

rows.label: Continuously compounded return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The log return. Additive across periods, which is why the option pricer and the projection fan work in it.

rows.label: Real return (Fisher, 3.0% inflation)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1. The exact form, not the subtraction.

rows.label: Sample standard deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Equal-weighted over the window, from weekly returns. The KPI card uses an exponentially weighted daily version that leans on recent days; the two differ when the recent past is calmer or wilder than the whole.

rows.label: Mean absolute deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: The average distance from the mean, without squaring. Less swayed by the worst days than the standard deviation.

rows.label: Downside deviation (target = cash rate)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Only the days below the target count. The risk a holder actually minds; the denominator of the Sortino ratio.

rows.label: Coefficient of variation (risk per unit of return)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Standard deviation over mean return. Lower is more return per unit of risk; the Sharpe ratio is its inverse with cash taken out.

rows.label: Skewness of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Negative: the big days are down days. Zero is symmetric. Equity indices usually run slightly negative.

rows.label: Excess kurtosis of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Above zero is fat tails: extreme days come more often than a normal distribution allows, so every normal-based VaR on this site is a floor.

rows.label: Sharpe ratio (cash 2.00%)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return over cash per unit of total risk. Total risk, so it is the right measure for the whole of someone's money.

rows.label: Sortino ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Sharpe with only downside deviation in the denominator. Flatters a book whose swings are mostly upward.

rows.label: Treynor ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return per unit of beta - systematic risk only. Right for a slice of a diversified whole, wrong for a concentrated book that carries the other kind.

rows.label: Jensen's alpha (CAPM, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Return above what beta alone would have earned. Not a t-statistic - the factor panel on Advice tests whether it is distinguishable from zero.

rows.label: M² (Modigliani, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The book's Sharpe ratio expressed as a return at the market's volatility, less the market. Positive means the risk-adjusted record beats the index in a unit a client can read.

rows.label: Information ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Active return over tracking error. Above 0.5 over several years is what an active manager would put on a slide.

rows.label: Tracking error, annualised
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: How far this book wanders from the index. Large is fine on purpose and expensive by accident.

rows.label: Up-market capture (weeks)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The book's return in the index's up days, over the index's. Above 100 gains more than the market when it rises.

rows.label: Down-market capture (weeks)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The same in the index's down days. Above 100 loses more than the market when it falls - the asymmetry to want is up above 100 and down below it.

rows.label: Beta (sample, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Covariance with the market over the market's variance, on weekly returns so the Frankfurt and New York closes land in the same bar.

rows.label: R² - share of variance that is the market
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The rest is nonsystematic: the part diversification would remove and the market does not pay for.

rows.label: Systematic share of total variance (β²σ²ₘ / σ²)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Same idea from the single-index model. Under the CAPM only this share earns a premium; the remainder is risk carried for free.

rows.label: Roy's safety-first ratio (threshold -0.0%)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk under the normal distribution
rows.what: Standard deviations of room above the return the goal needs. The optimal portfolio under safety-first is the one that maximises it.

rows.label: Probability of a year below the threshold (normal model)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk under the normal distribution
rows.what: Assumes normal returns; with fat tails the true figure is higher.

textbook.verdict: Compounded at 12.8% a year against the index's 12.2%, with 2.6 points a year lost to volatility drag against the index's 1.8. At the index's volatility the record is worth -0.7 points a year against it (M²), and Jensen's alpha is +0.0% - a point estimate, not a proof; the factor panel says whether it is real. Captures 110% of the index's up weeks and 111% of its down weeks - the wrong asymmetry: it gives back more than it takes. Excess kurtosis 0.5: tails close to normal over this window. 87% of the variance is the market; the other 13% is nonsystematic risk the CAPM says is carried without a premium. On a normal model there is a 25% chance of a year below the -0.0% the goal needs, against 23% for the index.
textbook.caveat: Sample statistics on weekly euro returns at today's weights, equal-weighted over the window, as the standard textbook formulas define them - so they will not match the KPI cards exactly, which use an exponentially weighted daily volatility. Weekly because the Frankfurt-listed index line and the US names close hours apart, and daily data splits each co-movement across two bars. Cash rate is the ECB deposit rate; the market is the S&P 500 line this book holds.

researchViews.caveat: Expected returns start at CAPM - beta, net of fees and the wrapper's tax - and the research is blended in as Black-Litterman views. Each signal's size is the published effect, halved because premia shrink after publication, shrunk further towards this book's own scored record as it accumulates: the prior counts for 40 observations and the local record for however many it has, so the view slides from the literature's to this book's rather than switching. Views are held at 25% confidence, which is deliberately low: the point is to tilt the optimiser towards what the accounts say, not to let a public-data signal run the portfolio. A name can still move further than its own view, because the blend runs through the covariance: several bearish views on correlated names push each other further than any one of them would alone.

current.verdict: Market beta 0.44: for every 1% the world index moves, this book moves about 0.44%. The market alone explains 92% of the book's weekly variance; market plus style explains 92%. The tilts that are real, not noise: dollar +0.08. The residual - what selection added - annualises to +0.9%, which is not distinguishable from zero. rows.label: Holding-period return, whole window
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: Total return over 5.0 years, compounded. The one number that cannot be annualised away.

rows.label: Arithmetic mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The mean weekly return, compounded to a year. The right expectation for a single period ahead; the wrong one for many.

rows.label: Geometric mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The compound rate the money actually grew at. Always at or below the arithmetic mean; the gap is volatility drag, about half the variance.

rows.label: Arithmetic less geometric (volatility drag)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: What the swings cost the compounding. This is the number the 'smoothest ride' mix on Advice is buying down.

rows.label: Continuously compounded return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The log return. Additive across periods, which is why the option pricer and the projection fan work in it.

rows.label: Real return (Fisher, 3.0% inflation)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1. The exact form, not the subtraction.

rows.label: Sample standard deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Equal-weighted over the window, from weekly returns. The KPI card uses an exponentially weighted daily version that leans on recent days; the two differ when the recent past is calmer or wilder than the whole.

rows.label: Mean absolute deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: The average distance from the mean, without squaring. Less swayed by the worst days than the standard deviation.

rows.label: Downside deviation (target = cash rate)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Only the days below the target count. The risk a holder actually minds; the denominator of the Sortino ratio.

rows.label: Coefficient of variation (risk per unit of return)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Standard deviation over mean return. Lower is more return per unit of risk; the Sharpe ratio is its inverse with cash taken out.

rows.label: Skewness of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Negative: the big days are down days. Zero is symmetric. Equity indices usually run slightly negative.

rows.label: Excess kurtosis of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Above zero is fat tails: extreme days come more often than a normal distribution allows, so every normal-based VaR on this site is a floor.

rows.label: Sharpe ratio (cash 2.00%)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return over cash per unit of total risk. Total risk, so it is the right measure for the whole of someone's money.

rows.label: Sortino ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Sharpe with only downside deviation in the denominator. Flatters a book whose swings are mostly upward.

rows.label: Treynor ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return per unit of beta - systematic risk only. Right for a slice of a diversified whole, wrong for a concentrated book that carries the other kind.

rows.label: Jensen's alpha (CAPM, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Return above what beta alone would have earned. Not a t-statistic - the factor panel on Advice tests whether it is distinguishable from zero.

rows.label: M² (Modigliani, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The book's Sharpe ratio expressed as a return at the market's volatility, less the market. Positive means the risk-adjusted record beats the index in a unit a client can read.

rows.label: Information ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Active return over tracking error. Above 0.5 over several years is what an active manager would put on a slide.

rows.label: Tracking error, annualised
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: How far this book wanders from the index. Large is fine on purpose and expensive by accident.

textbook.verdict: Compounded at 6.1% a year against the index's 12.2%, with 0.3 points a year lost to volatility drag against the index's 1.8. At the index's volatility the record is worth -1.4 points a year against it (M²), and Jensen's alpha is -0.4% - a point estimate, not a proof; the factor panel says whether it is real. Captures 42% of the index's up weeks and 40% of its down weeks - the right asymmetry. Excess kurtosis 0.5: tails close to normal over this window. 92% of the variance is the market; the other 8% is nonsystematic risk the CAPM says is carried without a premium. On a normal model there is a 36% chance of a year below the 3.5% the goal needs, against 30% for the index.
textbook.caveat: Sample statistics on weekly euro returns at today's weights, equal-weighted over the window, as the standard textbook formulas define them - so they will not match the KPI cards exactly, which use an exponentially weighted daily volatility. Weekly because the Frankfurt-listed index line and the US names close hours apart, and daily data splits each co-movement across two bars. Cash rate is the ECB deposit rate; the market is the S&P 500 line this book holds.

researchViews.caveat: Expected returns start at CAPM - beta, net of fees and the wrapper's tax - and the research is blended in as Black-Litterman views. Each signal's size is the published effect, halved because premia shrink after publication, shrunk further towards this book's own scored record as it accumulates: the prior counts for 40 observations and the local record for however many it has, so the view slides from the literature's to this book's rather than switching. Views are held at 25% confidence, which is deliberately low: the point is to tilt the optimiser towards what the accounts say, not to let a public-data signal run the portfolio. A name can still move further than its own view, because the blend runs through the covariance: several bearish views on correlated names push each other further than any one of them would alone.

rows.label: Holding-period return, whole window
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: Total return over 5.0 years, compounded. The one number that cannot be annualised away.

rows.label: Arithmetic mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The mean weekly return, compounded to a year. The right expectation for a single period ahead; the wrong one for many.

rows.label: Geometric mean return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The compound rate the money actually grew at. Always at or below the arithmetic mean; the gap is volatility drag, about half the variance.

rows.label: Arithmetic less geometric (volatility drag)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: What the swings cost the compounding. This is the number the 'smoothest ride' mix on Advice is buying down.

rows.label: Continuously compounded return, annualised
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: The log return. Additive across periods, which is why the option pricer and the projection fan work in it.

rows.label: Real return (Fisher, 3.0% inflation)
rows.ref: Rates and returns
rows.what: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1. The exact form, not the subtraction.

rows.label: Sample standard deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Equal-weighted over the window, from weekly returns. The KPI card uses an exponentially weighted daily version that leans on recent days; the two differ when the recent past is calmer or wilder than the whole.

rows.label: Mean absolute deviation, annualised
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: The average distance from the mean, without squaring. Less swayed by the worst days than the standard deviation.

rows.label: Downside deviation (target = cash rate)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Only the days below the target count. The risk a holder actually minds; the denominator of the Sortino ratio.

rows.label: Coefficient of variation (risk per unit of return)
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Standard deviation over mean return. Lower is more return per unit of risk; the Sharpe ratio is its inverse with cash taken out.

rows.label: Skewness of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Negative: the big days are down days. Zero is symmetric. Equity indices usually run slightly negative.

rows.label: Excess kurtosis of weekly returns
rows.ref: Statistical measures of returns
rows.what: Above zero is fat tails: extreme days come more often than a normal distribution allows, so every normal-based VaR on this site is a floor.

rows.label: Sharpe ratio (cash 2.00%)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return over cash per unit of total risk. Total risk, so it is the right measure for the whole of someone's money.

rows.label: Sortino ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Sharpe with only downside deviation in the denominator. Flatters a book whose swings are mostly upward.

rows.label: Treynor ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Excess return per unit of beta - systematic risk only. Right for a slice of a diversified whole, wrong for a concentrated book that carries the other kind.

rows.label: Jensen's alpha (CAPM, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Return above what beta alone would have earned. Not a t-statistic - the factor panel on Advice tests whether it is distinguishable from zero.

rows.label: M² (Modigliani, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The book's Sharpe ratio expressed as a return at the market's volatility, less the market. Positive means the risk-adjusted record beats the index in a unit a client can read.

rows.label: Information ratio
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Active return over tracking error. Above 0.5 over several years is what an active manager would put on a slide.

rows.label: Tracking error, annualised
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: How far this book wanders from the index. Large is fine on purpose and expensive by accident.

rows.label: Up-market capture (weeks)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The book's return in the index's up days, over the index's. Above 100 gains more than the market when it rises.

rows.label: Down-market capture (weeks)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The same in the index's down days. Above 100 loses more than the market when it falls - the asymmetry to want is up above 100 and down below it.

rows.label: Beta (sample, vs the S&P 500 line)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Covariance with the market over the market's variance, on weekly returns so the Frankfurt and New York closes land in the same bar.

rows.label: R² - share of variance that is the market
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: The rest is nonsystematic: the part diversification would remove and the market does not pay for.

rows.label: Systematic share of total variance (β²σ²ₘ / σ²)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk and return, part two
rows.what: Same idea from the single-index model. Under the CAPM only this share earns a premium; the remainder is risk carried for free.

rows.label: Roy's safety-first ratio (threshold 1.6%)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk under the normal distribution
rows.what: Standard deviations of room above the return the goal needs. The optimal portfolio under safety-first is the one that maximises it.

rows.label: Probability of a year below the threshold (normal model)
rows.ref: Portfolio risk under the normal distribution
rows.what: Assumes normal returns; with fat tails the true figure is higher.

textbook.verdict: Compounded at 7.9% a year against the index's 12.2%, with 0.6 points a year lost to volatility drag against the index's 1.8. At the index's volatility the record is worth -0.4 points a year against it (M²), and Jensen's alpha is +0.7% - a point estimate, not a proof; the factor panel says whether it is real. Captures 51% of the index's up weeks and 48% of its down weeks - the right asymmetry. Excess kurtosis 0.1: tails close to normal over this window. 74% of the variance is the market; the other 26% is nonsystematic risk the CAPM says is carried without a premium. On a normal model there is a 26% chance of a year below the 1.6% the goal needs, against 26% for the index.
textbook.caveat: Sample statistics on weekly euro returns at today's weights, equal-weighted over the window, as the standard textbook formulas define them - so they will not match the KPI cards exactly, which use an exponentially weighted daily volatility. Weekly because the Frankfurt-listed index line and the US names close hours apart, and daily data splits each co-movement across two bars. Cash rate is the ECB deposit rate; the market is the S&P 500 line this book holds.

researchViews.caveat: Expected returns start at CAPM - beta, net of fees and the wrapper's tax - and the research is blended in as Black-Litterman views. Each signal's size is the published effect, halved because premia shrink after publication, shrunk further towards this book's own scored record as it accumulates: the prior counts for 40 observations and the local record for however many it has, so the view slides from the literature's to this book's rather than switching. Views are held at 25% confidence, which is deliberately low: the point is to tilt the optimiser towards what the accounts say, not to let a public-data signal run the portfolio. A name can still move further than its own view, because the blend runs through the covariance: several bearish views on correlated names push each other further than any one of them would alone.

committee.method: Eight members read the same evidence through different lenses and each put forward their best buy and their weakest holding. Every member then rated every other member's ideas from -5 to +5 by their own method - a buy by how much they like the line, a sale by how much they dislike it. Ideas are ranked by the mean rating. The CIO applies the gates the whole book has to respect - house calls, the mortgage glide path, conviction caps, trade size - and approves at most three.
committee.caveat: The members are rules, not people: the same evidence gives the same minutes. In this demo they sit on a fictional book with synthetic prices, and nothing here is investment advice.

research.attribution: Illustrative theme notes written for this demo. They describe generic portfolio-construction trade-offs, cite no third-party research and refer only to fictional instruments. Not investment advice.

ai.title: The AI / technology trade
ai.view: When a single theme drives most of a book, its holdings stop diversifying each other: a slowdown in the theme hits the companies, the sector funds and the index funds that are heavy in them at the same time. The growth and Sharpe mixes therefore cap the theme rather than let CAPM pile into the highest-beta lines.

em.title: Emerging markets
em.view: A cap-weighted emerging-markets index can be dominated by a handful of large technology names, so in this demo it is counted as part of the technology theme rather than as a separate diversifier.

gold.title: Gold
gold.view: Gold has no cash flow; it is held, if at all, for its behaviour in equity sell-offs. The stress-correlation column shows whether it actually did that in this book's synthetic history.

bonds.title: Bonds
bonds.view: Investment-grade bond funds lower volatility and usually, but not always, cushion equity falls - a simultaneous rate shock hits both.

dividend.title: Dividend strategies
dividend.view: A dividend tilt changes when returns arrive, not necessarily how large they are, and in some tax regimes distributions are taxed every year.

lessons.title: Size by conviction
lessons.rule: No company above 15% of the book, and 15% only when you are highly confident. Medium conviction is capped at 10%, low at 5%.

lessons.title: Think like a short seller
lessons.rule: Write down what could break each holding before the case for it.

lessons.title: Earnings over yield
lessons.rule: Prefer growing earnings to a high dividend; a yield without earnings behind it is a trap.

lessons.title: Recovery at the right price
lessons.rule: The losers worth holding are recovery or turnaround companies bought on attractive valuations.

lessons.title: Cut losers, let winners run
lessons.rule: Sell what is below trend first; trim what is working last.

lessons.title: One theme, one index
lessons.rule: Cap the AI / technology theme at 25% of the book and hold each index through one fund.
